Yesterday's reports indicated that Apple had once considered producing a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra, but later decided to abandon the idea.

Bloomberg pointed out three reasons behind this decision, one of which was not wanting to conflict with the stance Steve Jobs took when he launched the original iPhone. However, this is almost certainly not the decisive factor...

A shorter Apple Pencil that could be used with the iPhone Ultra does sound like an appealing idea on the surface. The device is essentially an iPhone that can transform into an iPad mini, so giving it some of the same capabilities is clearly a very reasonable thought.

Samsung equipped the Galaxy Note phablet with an S-Pen stylus as early as 2011 when it launched. The idea at the time was that the device could to some extent replace a paper notebook, and it did indeed have a loyal user base, surviving in the market for ten years until production ceased in 2021.

Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman listed three reasons why Apple ultimately abandoned this idea:

  • Placing the Pencil on the side of the device rather than the top would make the device feel awkward to hold
  • This would conflict with Jobs' view that a stylus is a poor substitute for the finger
  • It would leave unsightly marks on the screen

I don't think the first point would be the main consideration, since mounting the stylus on the top of the device is itself a possible solution. Although this would require designing the stylus to be very short, I believe it could still be made to work, albeit barely.

The second point also fails to convince me. What Jobs objected to was not the idea that smartphones could be used with a stylus, but rather that the models at the time had to rely on a stylus for operation. Making the iPhone practically operable by finger was the breakthrough back then.

In any case, Jobs also famously refused to adopt touchscreens on the Mac on the grounds of poor ergonomics, yet we currently still expect the upcoming MacBook Pro models to include touchscreen functionality, which shows that Apple is not afraid to overturn the past positions of its co-founder.

I believe what truly killed this idea was the third reason. The surface of a folding screen is inevitably far thinner and more flexible than the screens of existing devices. Reports indicate that Apple waited years before launching the first foldable iPhone because of concerns about the screen's appearance and durability. If an Apple Pencil were allowed to repeatedly scratch across the screen, both would be put at risk.

If Apple can resolve this issue in the future, would you like to see an Apple Pencil Mini designed for use with a future iPhone Ultra? Feel free to let us know in the comments section.
